sections.src: photo — hewn timbers are irregular, these are representative means
sections.postRange: 0.15-0.25 wide, each one different (hand-hewn salvage); 0.25 nominal used because it is what makes the wall run close out
sections._girtNote: 100 x 50 given - 50 mm through the wall, 100 mm deep. Was assumed 140 x 180.
sections.girtJoint: housed into the post, 6 x 10 mm screws
sections._girtJoint: OWNER 2026-08-21, and it CLOSES F10. The girt is let into the posts, not butted and screwed to their faces. That changes the load path from screws-in-shear to BEARING ON WOOD, which is what F10 was actually worried about - the finding read the joint as 4 x 6 mm screws that had to bite the post behind, and if they missed it there was no path at all. Numbers: brace delivers 3.92 kN, the along-girt component is 2.77 kN, bearing on the 50 x 100 girt end is 0.55 MPa against fc,90,d 1.73 - factor 3.1. The screws are now a retaining fixing, and 6 x 10 mm carry it alone anyway: 4.10 kN design each (EN 1995 8.2.2 mode f, 50 mm side member, kmod 0.9, gammaM 1.3), 24.6 kN for six, factor 6.3.
sections._girtJointReversal: A housing works in COMPRESSION ONLY - it stops the girt being driven into the post, not pulled out of it. Racking reverses, so on the return gust the brace on that side goes into tension and the housing does nothing. That is fine here for two reasons: braced frames are designed compression-only, with the brace on the other hand picking up the reversed case, and the 6 x 10 mm screws cover it on their own at factor 6.3 regardless. Worth knowing before anyone leaves a brace out of a bay.
sections._girtJointToConfirm: HOUSING DEPTH is not recorded. Anything from about 25 mm gives a positive joint without eating the 179 mm post; a 10 mm locating notch still bears the same 0.55 MPa but is less forgiving of a sloppy shoulder. Measure one and write it down.
sections._thickness: Walls are 150 mm through. Post along-wall dimension 179 mm is the average that makes the measured bays close on 9.31 m.
sections._heights: Course heights come from heights.sillCourse / heights.plateCourse ONLY. They used to be duplicated here at 150 and disagreed with the 185 there, leaving a 70 mm gap between sill and post.
sections._rafter: 50x150, dropped from 50x250 on 2026-08-15. The purlins break the 5.10 m backspan into two 2.55 m spans, so the rafter was never close to working: at 150 it runs 3.05 MPa against 16.6 (factor 5.4) and deflects 1.0 mm against an 8.5 mm limit. It is also BETTER for lateral-torsional buckling - h/b drops from 5.0 to 3.0 and kcrit goes from 0.827 to 0.992, so no intermediate restraint is needed. Ridge drops 0.17 m.

bays._note: 9 posts, 8 clear gaps summing 7.70 m. With a 9.31 m wall that makes the posts average 179 mm - inside your 150-250 mm range. The 7-gap reading needed 326 mm posts, so there is an eighth gap of about 1 m.

piers.material: cast concrete with steel mesh reinforcement
piers.src: given 2026-08-15 - CORRECTS the earlier reading. The model previously had 250x250 dry-laid clay brick sitting on grade, taken from photographs. It is 300 mm diameter cast concrete, 1.2 m deep, reinforced.
piers._capacity: Base area 0.0707 m2, shaft 1.13 m2. At 1.2 m depth in Latvian sandy/silty till allowable base pressure is 150-250 kPa, not the 50-75 kPa available at grade. End bearing 10.6-17.7 kN plus shaft friction 17-28 kN = 28-46 kN per pile, against 9.8 kN on a plain pile and 19.1 kN under a strut frame at ULS. Factor 1.4 to 2.4 on the worst pile.
piers._frost: 1.2 m IS the Latvian frost depth, so the base sits at the frost line rather than comfortably below it - the code minimum, not a margin. The mechanism that matters for a slender pile is ADFREEZE on the shaft, not heave under the base, and it threatens the LIGHTLY loaded piles, not the heavy ones. That is the opposite of the settlement risk. Mitigation: a smooth shaft, or a bituminous/polythene slip sleeve over the top 1.0 m.
piers._supersedes: F1 and F2 were both written on the brick-on-grade premise and are now wrong.
piers._sillDpc: AS BUILT, owner 2026-08-21: bituminous membrane laid between the pile head and the sill, at every pile. Closes the last open item in F5 - the capillary barrier was pierced at all 24 sill anchors (M14 x 300 as built) and wanted a DPC pad at each pile head. This is not a detail to file under damp-proofing and forget: it is what keeps the frame in SERVICE CLASS 2, and at class 3 kdef goes 0.80 to 2.00 and the tie fails on deflection at 36.6 mm. Every kmod and kdef in the model rests on it.
piers._dpcNotTheSleeve: IT IS NOT THE FROST SLEEVE, and the two get confused because both are bituminous. The DPC is a horizontal layer ON TOP of the pile head, against damp rising into the sill. The F2 slip sleeve wraps the OUTSIDE of the buried shaft over the top 1.0 m, against frozen soil bonding to it and dragging the pile up. Different surface, different mechanism, and a layer on the pile head cannot reach the one that matters: adfreeze grips the sides, below grade. F2 stays open.
piers._dpcAndShear: The slip plane the membrane introduces at the sill is harmless. Base shear goes through the sill anchors in shear - 2.56 kN per pile against 20 kN on an M14 x 300 - not through friction between timber and concrete, so losing that friction costs nothing.

sillAnchor.src: given 2026-08-15, size confirmed by the owner 2026-08-21 - lowest wall course screwed into the concrete with M14 x 300
sillAnchor._asBuilt: M14 x 300, not the M12 previously recorded. For WIND this is hugely over-specified and that question is closed: stability.md has hold-down at 0.77 kN per windward pile against 8.00 (factor 10.4) and shear at 2.56 against 20.00 (factor 7.8). An M14 at that embedment beats both several times over.
sillAnchor._doesNotCloseF2: IT DOES NOT ANSWER F2, AND IT SLIGHTLY WORSENS THE CONSEQUENCE. F2 is about the GROUND, not the anchor: the piles bear AT 1.2 m, which is the Latvian frost line rather than below it, and the mechanism that matters is ADFREEZE on the shaft - 28-42 kN of uplift on a lightly loaded pile. Nothing about a bigger anchor reduces that load; it only decides which link breaks. The binding limit was never the anchor steel, it is the WASHER BEARING ON THE SILL - 5.96 kN at 60x60, 10.8 kN at 80x80, against fc,90,d 1.73. So with an M12 there was at least a chance the anchor let go and relieved the frame, a crude fuse. An M14 x 300 removes that fuse and guarantees the SILL is what splits. The slip sleeve over the top 1.0 m of every shaft is what removes the 28-42 kN in the first place, and it is now the only thing standing between the anchor and the sill.
sillAnchor._capacity: Demand is trivial: 1.07 kN per anchor in uplift (F6 door-open, 9.7 kN per long wall over ~9 anchors) and 1.81 kN in shear (16.3 kN base shear per wall). An M12 in C20/25 gives 7-10 kN tension and 6-8 kN shear.
sillAnchor._washer: USE 60x60 WASHERS MINIMUM. The anchor is not the weak link - the washer bearing on the sill is. At fc,90,d 1.73 MPa a 40x40 washer crushes the timber at 2.50 kN and a 50x50 at 4.06 kN, both below what the anchor can deliver. 60x60 gives 5.96 kN, 80x80 gives 10.8 kN.

piers._frostNowMatters: Anchoring the sill to the piles REMOVES the building's ability to ride out frost heave. Loose on dry-laid brick a heaving support just lifts off the frame. Bolted, 28-42 kN of adfreeze uplift goes straight into the sill - and nothing in the connection stops that: a 60x60 washer yields at 6.0 kN. Either the sill splits, the anchor pulls, or the corner lifts. The slip sleeve over the top 1.0 m of shaft is therefore no longer optional; it is what protects the anchors. Fit it before backfill is settled.

joists.src: given - 100x250 ties, flush with the outer wall faces, notched 50 mm each end. NOT YET INSTALLED as of 2026-08-14 - still in the yard, so they draw on stock.
joists._spacing: 700 mm CENTRES = 600 mm CLEAR. AS BUILT - the owner set the ties out at 700 and reported it 2026-08-21. The driver is the insulation: it comes in 600 x 1000 mm packs, and 600 clear between 100 mm ties is what takes a pack without cutting. History: one tie per post at 1151 mm deflected 45.6 mm (L/132) against a 24 mm limit; 576 mm gave 22.8 mm; 600 mm centres gave 23.8 mm. THIS SPACING DOES NOT PASS ON THE MODEL'S ORIGINAL BASIS - see _deflection. It passes on the knee braces acting as props, which is now a REQUIRED detail, not an optional one.
joists._deflection: THE ONE THING TO GET RIGHT ON THIS FLOOR. Three ways to model the same tie at 700 mm centres, w = 1391 N/m, 100x250, limit L/250 = 24 mm:  (a) simply supported over the modelled 6.00 m, which is what every earlier figure in this project used: 16.4 mm instant, 27.3 mm final - 14% OVER, L/220.  (b) simply supported over the TRUE bearing centres, 5.85 m: 14.8 -> 24.6 mm, 2.5% over.  (c) propped by the knee braces at +-2.53 m, so a 5.06 m span with 0.47 m overhangs: 7.9 -> 13.2 mm, factor 1.8 - PASSES with real margin. The truth is between (b) and (c) and the bounds straddle the limit, which is exactly why the model was conservative before. The BEARING SEAT on the knee brace is what turns (c) from an argument into a fact. Fit it and the floor is 13 mm; leave the braces screwed-only and the honest answer is somewhere in 13-25 mm and you cannot say which.
joists._otherJobs: The tie does three more jobs and 700 mm centres was checked against all of them 2026-08-21. BENDING: 8.41 MPa against 14.8 unpropped, 5.98 propped - factor 1.8 either way, bending was never the problem. RAFTER TIE: horizontal demand per tie end goes 3.13 -> 3.80 kN against 11.8 kN of bracket, factor 3.1 (was 3.8). STRUT BEARING: unchanged, 8 struts per side whatever the tie count, 0.93 MPa against fc,90,d 1.73. PLATE SPLICES: F16a is GONE - at 700 mm the nearest tie to any splice is 150 mm, against the 98 mm EN 1995 wants and the 50 mm that 600 mm centres produced.
joists._closeOut: 9.30 m outer to outer, end ties flush, so the centreline run is 9.20 m, and 9.20 does not divide by 700 either. The remainder goes into the LAST bay against the back gable, which becomes 800 mm centres - and that is the bay whose tie is omitted for the stair, so the odd dimension lands in the one opening where nothing spans. Result: eleven bays at exactly 600 mm CLEAR, a stair bay 1.50 m centre to centre and 1.40 m clear, and 13 ties. Setout from the front outer face: 50, 750, 1450, 2150, 2850, 3550, 4250, 4950, 5650, 6350, 7050, 7750, [8450 - rafter and tail joist, no tie], 9250.
joists._insulationClear: 600 mm CLEAR in every loft-floor bay, which is what the 600 x 1000 mm insulation packs are bought to fill. This is the reason for the spacing. NOTE the packs will sit in a true 600 gap rather than friction-fit - a batt made for 600 mm CENTRES expects about 550 clear and grips. In a floor that does not matter, the pack sits on the ceiling below. In a ceiling plane it would, so if any of this insulation ends up overhead rather than underfoot, net it or fit retainers. Between the RAFTERS the packs friction-fit properly: 700 mm rafter centres on a 50 mm rafter leaves 650 clear, so there the 600 pack is LOOSE - use 600 centres on any ceiling grid, not 700.
joists._offPost: At 600 mm the ties do not land on posts; posts are at 1151 mm, so roughly every other tie lands mid-bay and the plate carries it. Plate 150x185 over a 1.15 m bay under a 3.83 kN reaction runs at 1.3 MPa against 14.8 - fine.
joists._spliceClash: RECOMPUTED 2026-08-21 for the 600 mm setout, and it got tighter. Plate splices are as-built and do not move: lower -0.65, upper -1.65, +1.35, +3.35. Ties now land at -1.60 and +1.40 - 50 mm from an upper-layer splice, against 72 and 79 mm before. EN 1995 wants 7d = 98 mm end distance for a loaded M14. It is still not critical for the same reason as before: the LOWER layer is continuous at both of those stations (its only splice is at -0.65, a metre away), so the load has a path. Two things make it less of a problem than it looks: the tie-to-wall connection is now a bracket pair, not the 2 x M14 through-rod that F16a was written about, and the rafter-seat M14 goes rafter-to-tie, not into the plate. STILL strap those two splices (F16 detail, 4 x 6x200 each side, staggered over 600 mm) BEFORE the ties go down.
joists._endNotch: 30 mm, not 50 - owner 2026-08-21. The tie is let into the 50 mm LEVELLING COURSE, not down into the plate below it, so the 185 mm plate course keeps its full depth and there is 20 mm of levelling course still under the tie. The tie therefore sits 20 mm HIGHER than the model had it, not lower. Everything keyed to it moves up 20 mm: tie top 3.840 -> 3.860, loft floor 3.880 -> 3.900, brace ledger 3.166 -> 3.186. Loft headroom loses 20 mm (3.889 -> 3.869 at the centre) and the stair riser gains 1 mm (175.2 -> 176.2 over 21). Nothing near a limit moves.
joists._cantilever: COGGED LIP, owner 2026-08-21, and it is a better detail than the one it replaces. The ties came in at roughly 6.15-6.20 m against a 6.00 m building, and rather than trim them flush the owner is cutting so about 50 mm is left projecting past each OUTER wall face, dropped below the bearing plane so it HOOKS OVER the wall. That gives the rafter-thrust spread a path in BEARING ON WOOD instead of through fasteners: 3.80 kN per tie end at 700 mm spacing, on a 50 x 100 lip, is 0.76 MPa against fc,90,d 1.73 (factor 2.3) and 0.76 against fv,d 2.77 in shear along the tie (factor 3.6). Deeper is better and nearly free while you have the saw out - 60 mm gives 2.7, 80 mm gives 3.6.
joists._lipDoesNotDoUplift: THE LIP DOES NOT HOLD THE TIE DOWN. It stops the walls SPREADING; it does nothing against the tie lifting off, and uplift is no longer a wind-only case - the knee-brace props take more than the whole floor, so the tie ends carry 4.01 kN of permanent uplift (stability.md). The 2 x M14 at every tie end stay MANDATORY, factor 3.5. A lip is not a substitute for a hold-down and it would be easy to think it was.
joists._lipMeetsTheCladding: 26 lips project 50 mm past the outer wall face, right at the head of the wall and squarely in the rainscreen plane - the wall battens are 25 x 50 on that face. Do NOT notch the cladding around 26 of them; that is 26 details and 26 places for water to get behind. Stop the cladding below the tie line and close the head with one continuous trim or soffit above it. One horizontal line instead of 26 cut-outs. The lips themselves are fine for weather - the eaves overhang 0.53 m horizontally, so they sit well inside the drip line.

plateOverhang.src: measured - lower plate course projects 0.50 m past each gable, upper 1.00 m.
plateOverhang._cutBack: CANCELLED 2026-08-21 - the verge stays at 1.0 m, so nothing gets cut back. This note used to say the upper course had to come back to 0.50 m at all four corners, which was work already done being undone. It is not happening, and that is the cheapest decision of the day. WHAT THE WALL TOP ACTUALLY DOES at the gable, owner 2026-08-21: lower plate course projects 0.50 m, upper plate course 1.00 m, and the 50 mm levelling course on top of it also 1.00 m. Only the lower course stops short.
plateOverhang._notStructural: F9 was about a 4.0 m purlin cantilever with NO gable bearing: 38.7 MPa and 113 mm droop. The gable studs fixed that. At 1.0 m the verge cantilever ran 2.4 MPa and 0.4 mm - comfortable. Shortening to 0.50 m is a material and appearance decision, not a structural fix.

opening.src: width given (~3 m). Height scaled from the approved front elevation, which shows an opening ~2.6 m wide and ~3.1 m tall in a 3.70 m wall — CONFIRM height on site.
opening.lintel: none - the single 220x185 front plate course spans the 3 m opening

door.type: automatic rise-up - sectional overhead or roller shutter
door._headroom: THE CLASH. Opening head is at 3.370 and the tie underside at 3.610, so the door gear gets 240 mm - and only 85 mm before it reaches the lintel underside at 3.455. A standard-lift sectional door wants 300-450 mm above the opening for the torsion shaft and the curved track. A ROLLER SHUTTER is worse: a 2.8 m curtain rolls to a barrel 350-450 mm across and does not fit at all. This has to be settled BEFORE the opening is trimmed, because two of the three fixes change the carpentry.
door._options: (1) LOW-HEADROOM SECTIONAL KIT - double horizontal track, front-mounted shaft, fits in about 180-200 mm. Standard product, no change to the building, and the one to price first. (2) DROP THE OPENING HEAD. 2.8 -> 2.5 m gives 520 mm of gear space and costs 300 mm of door height; the 270 mm wall strip above the head grows to 570. (3) FACE-FIX A ROLLER OUTSIDE in a hood - keeps full opening height but puts the barrel in the rainscreen, clashes with the cladding grid and the entrance jamb battens, and exposes the gear. Roller shutter internally is NOT an option at 220 mm.
door._tracks: Horizontal tracks run back 3.3-3.5 m at about 3.40, i.e. 190 mm below the tie undersides, crossing the first 5-6 ties. At 700 mm centres there is an anchor point every 700 mm, so hang them off the TIES - never off the loft deck, and never off one tie alone: spread each hanger pair over two. The ties are propped members already running 12.0 mm of a 24 mm limit (F7/F24), and a track hanger is a permanent point load on them. Load is small - a 3.0 x 2.8 m insulated leaf is 80-130 kg, so 0.3-0.6 kN per hanger - but it is not zero and it lands inside the propped span.
door._header: The torsion shaft brackets bolt to the lintel, which over the opening is a SINGLE 220x185 plate course carrying the gable above (F8). Through-bolt them; do not screw into the underside of a member that is already the lintel. The shaft delivers roughly the whole leaf weight to two brackets when the door is shut.
door._openInStorms: OWNER OPERATING RULE, 2026-08-21: the door is not left open in high wind. EN 1991-1-4 7.2.9 recognises this - a dominant opening that is shut during severe storms is an ACCIDENTAL design situation, gQ 1.0 rather than 1.5, not a persistent one. Recorded as a design assumption because it is one: if the building ever changes hands or use, the next owner inherits a frame checked on the promise that somebody shuts the door.
door._windNumbers: It was never the governing case anyway, which is why this changes nothing. Net uplift per rafter foot against 8 kN of strap: 1.88 kN sealed at cpi +0.2 and gQ 1.5 (what stability.py uses), 1.78 kN door-open accidental at cpi +0.6 and gQ 1.0 - LOWER than the sealed persistent case - and 3.08 kN, factor 2.6, if you insisted on treating door-open as persistent. Sill anchors are 3.8-4.0 kN per M12 against 7-10 kN on every reading. Nothing in the frame is sized by the door.
door._manualOverride: Owner 2026-08-21: the doors have a manual failsafe close. That closes the gap the operating rule above would otherwise leave - the rule no longer depends on the grid being up, so 'shut in high wind' is an assumption somebody can actually keep during the power cut a storm brings with it. It is the reason openInStorms = false is a fair assumption rather than an optimistic one.
door._wind: A manual override does NOT cover the other failure, because it is a different one: the leaf shut, and wind pushing on 8.4 m2 of it. Design pressure on a windward face is qp x (cpe + cpi) = 0.557 x 1.1 = 0.61 kPa, so the door wants EN 12424 CLASS 3 (700 Pa); Class 2 is 450 Pa and is under it. A 3 m leaf usually needs the maker's wind-bracing struts to reach Class 3 - ask for them by name, they are an option, not standard. This is a line on the order, not a change to the building: nothing in the frame is sized by the door either way.
door._notAShearPanel: A rise-up door carries NO in-plane shear - it is a curtain on tracks. It does nothing for F25, and the 3 m of front gable it fills stays a hole as far as racking is concerned.

opening._jambPiles: AS BUILT, owner 2026-08-21: each side of the entrance stands on THREE piles counting the corner, not the two the 1.2 m grid gave. Drawn evenly over the 1.5 m from jamb to corner - 1.500, 2.250, 3.000 - so one lands directly under each jamb. That is what F8 and F23 were asking for and it closes both: the jambs bear on 1.2 m piles like the rest of the frame instead of standing on a ground-bearing slab that heaves independently of it.
opening._jambPileConsequence: One thing it adds. The four new piles are LIGHTLY loaded - about 3.5 kN each from the header - and adfreeze threatens the lightly loaded piles, not the heavy ones (F2). Slip-sleeve these four along with the rest, and do not skip them on the grounds that they carry least.

roof.src: given - rafters 50x250x6.0 m, bearing 50 mm on the top wall beam. Backspan to the wall is 5.10 m, leaving 0.90 m of tail past it.
roof._ridgeNote: 11.30 m = 9.30 m building + 1.00 m verge each end. REVERTED to 1.0 m on 2026-08-21: the owner confirms the verge is staying at 1 m, which is what the plate courses were built for. It had been shortened to 0.50 m on 2026-08-15. The approved drawings show 0.50 m, so this is a second departure from the permit envelope alongside the ridge height (F14) - it is not a setback problem, the boundary is 7 m away, but the drawings no longer describe the building.
roof._setout: One rafter beside each SETOUT station, so the rafters run at exactly 600 mm centres like the ties, and there is a rafter beside the station at +3.80 even though no tie is built there. Every rafter foot has a direct thrust path into a tie rather than going via the plate, except the one at the stair station, which goes into the plate as it always did at the omitted tie.
roof._rafterCloseOut: The 600 mm grid runs out against the back gable and the widest rafter bay in the roof becomes 650 mm - not 800, because the last rafter sits on the INNER face of the end tie while the rest sit on the outer face, which gives 75 mm back. Checked 2026-08-21 and it is nowhere near close: 50x150 rafter goes 3.05 -> 3.44 MPa against 16.6 (factor 4.8) and 1.0 -> 1.13 mm against an 8.5 mm limit; 25x100 battens at 300 mm centres over 650 go to about 1.1 MPa against 16.6. The purlin bears on the gable 0.5 m away, so nothing accumulates there. Verge close-outs are 575 mm, tighter than the grid, which is the harmless direction.
roof._battenModule: 600 mm rafter centres make a 6.0 m batten EXACTLY 10 bays with zero waste. At 576 it was 5.76 m used out of 6.0 - 4% thrown away, and the take-off had to be corrected from 63 boards to 66 for it. That correction goes away.
roof.ridgeDetail: Rafters cut square at the top so the outer top corners meet; the triangle below is cut off and the rafters lap onto the 50x250x11 m ridge purlin, screwed through.

battens._note: 25x100 at 300 mm. Changed from 20x100 on 2026-08-15. Two reasons: sheet screws bite 25 mm instead of 20 - at ~200 mm rib spacing most fixings fall BETWEEN counter-battens, so the batten is all they get - and it puts the whole job on ONE thickness (25x100 roof battens, 25x50 counter-battens, 25x50 wall battens) instead of three to keep apart on site.
battens._noMixing: Battens set the plane the sheeting lands on. A 5 mm step where 20 mm meets 25 mm telegraphs through the sheet as visible waves and preloads the fixings at the step. You cannot mix batten thicknesses on one slope - this is a defect, not a tolerance.
battens._screws: 25 mm gives proper hold. At 20 mm the numbers passed - 0.05 kN per screw over a 200x298 mm tributary, 0.15 kN in the corner suction zones, against 800-1200 N pull-over - but it was the thinnest link in the fixing chain.
battens.roofMembrane: breather membrane over the rafters, under the counter-battens, drained to outside the wall line
battens._roofMembrane: OWNER 2026-08-21 and it is the F21 answer: the membrane catches condensate off the underside of the steel and guides it out of the building rather than letting it drip inside. Standard cold-roof detail, and coherent with the 25 mm counter-batten cavity already specified. THE DISCHARGE POINT IS THE WHOLE DETAIL - the membrane must run out OVER the fascia into the gutter, outside the wall line. Stopped short at the wall top it delivers every drop into the eaves, onto the wall plate and the tie ends, which is the one zone that cannot be inspected once the loft is decked. Laps shingle-style, upper sheet over lower. Breather/HPV type, NOT a vapour barrier - a closed membrane condenses on its own underside. Same product on the walls behind the vertical 25x50 battens is correct.
battens._counterBatten: 25 x 50 - width halved 2026-08-15. The DEPTH is the only structural dimension: it IS the ventilation cavity and must stay >= 25 mm (F21). The width only has to take the batten screws, so 50 is enough and it halves the volume. NOT mixing with the 20 mm battens - different member, different plane, they never meet edge to edge.
battens._alignment: At 50 wide on a 50 wide rafter there is ZERO setting-out tolerance - the counter-batten must land square on the rafter or the fixing misses. Screw the counter-batten to the rafter first, where you can see both, then the battens to the counter-batten.
battens._sheetFixings: Sheet screws land on the BATTEN, and at 200 mm rib spacing most of them fall between counter-battens - so they get 20 mm of timber, not 45. That is fine: uplift per screw is about 0.05 kN over a 200 x 298 mm tributary, even at the 0.84 kPa door-open worst case, and roughly 0.15 kN in the corner suction zones. Well inside pull-out from 20 mm.
battens._cutting: Batten joints land ON a rafter line, one piece ending at the rafter centre and the next starting there. Rafter lines are at 600 mm, so every piece is a WHOLE NUMBER OF BAYS - and a 6 m board is EXACTLY 10 bays, 6.00 m, zero waste. At 576 it was 5.76 m of every 6 m board, 4% thrown away, and the take-off carried a correction from 63 boards to 66 to cover it. That correction is gone: divide the length by 6 and buy that.
battens._joints: 18 bays per run, so one 5.76 m piece + one 4.55 m piece = 1 joint per run, 42 joints. STAGGER them between adjacent runs so they do not line up in a column up the slope.
battens._jointPads: A 50 mm counter-batten CANNOT take a butt joint: two batten ends meeting on it get 25 mm of bearing each and the screw sits ~12 mm from the end, which splits. A 4-5 mm screw wants 10-15d = 50-75 mm. Screw a 300 mm offcut of 25x50 alongside at each joint - 100 mm of bearing, 50 mm end distance each side. 42 pads x 300 mm = 12.6 m, 3 extra boards.
battens._cost: EUR 119. Only EUR 68 of that is the thicker section; the other EUR 51 is the owner's 57.6 m of 20x100 becoming unusable - you cannot mix 20 and 25 in one roof plane, the step telegraphs through the sheet. The 20 mm is not wasted, it goes to trim, soffit or internal work.

purlins.src: given: 2 purlins 50x250 at mid-rafter. No new cross beams - struts land on the wall plate at every tie beam, so the purlin load bypasses the ties.
purlins._spans: With gable bearing at +/-4.5 and frames at -3,-1,1,3 the purlin spans are 1.5, 2.0, 2.0, 2.0, 1.5 m plus a 1.0 m verge cantilever. Max 2.0 m.
purlins.support: vertical post on the tie under each purlin with a 100x100 head block, plus a diagonal strut out to the wall and a collar tying the two purlin lines together
purlins._note: 8 struts per slope, on 8 of the 9 tie beams.
purlins._strutFoot: Strut foot stands on the tie beam 100 mm in from the outer wall face, so it is fully bearing on the 100 mm wide tie while still sitting essentially over the wall.
purlins._strutBearing: Strut drops past the tie and bears on the wall plate beside it, so the tie carries no roof load at all. Ties are at 1.18 m centres and 100 mm wide, leaving 1.08 m of clear plate between each pair. Set to 'tie' to land on the tie instead (costs 0.72 kNm and 2.3 mm of sag).
purlins._sections: Purlins and ridge stay 50x250 - the rafters bear on them. Everything supporting them (struts, verticals, collars) is 100x100.
purlins._collar: 50x100, dropped from 100x100 2026-08-15. The collar carries about 2 kN axial and nothing else - no transverse load, nothing bears on it. At 2.37 m the 50x100 buckles at 8.7 kN, a factor of 4.4. The strut cannot follow it down: at 2.19 m a 50x100 gives 10.2 kN against a 9.3 kN demand, factor 1.1, so strutSection stays 100x100.
purlins._evened: Was 5. Raised to 8 so the load lands on 8 of the 9 posts instead of 5: strut post 12.3 -> 9.4 kN, pier 197 -> 151 kPa. Not needed for capacity - needed so a foundation that is staying as-is settles evenly. F17.
purlins._verticalOrientation: 100 mm ALONG the building, 50 across - and this is the whole detail, not a preference. The short piece under the purlin gives 100 x 50 = 5000 mm2 of seat under a purlin that is only 50 wide. Turned the other way it is 50 x 50 = 2500, the bearing goes 0.77 -> 1.54 MPa and the factor 2.2 -> 1.1. Same board, same cut, one turn of the wrist.
purlins._cutLengths: ROUND THEM IN OPPOSITE DIRECTIONS. Drawn heights are bar 1.595 and stem 1.845 off a tie top at 3.860, to a purlin underside of 5.455 and top of 5.705. The STEM rounds UP to 1.85 freely - it bears nothing, it is screwed to the purlin face. The BAR rounds DOWN to 1.59, or better, is scribed to fit. A bar 5 mm PROUD cannot compress 5 mm under a 6.89 kN reaction (it would take 172 kN at EA/L = 34.5 kN/mm), so the strut never touches: the bar takes 100% of the reaction instead of its 55% share and the tie goes 23.3 -> about 32 mm against a 24 mm limit. Five millimetres of tidiness costs the floor. Five millimetres SHORT is harmless the other way - the bar carries nothing, the strut carries the whole 6.89 kN, which is the pre-2026-08-21 design and still passes at 1.38 MPa head bearing against 1.73. Cut shy, scribe, and NEVER pack it up.
purlins._setoutFromWall: Measured in from the OUTER wall face along the tie, less 150 for the inner face. BAR centre 1500, occupying 1475-1525 - the same footprint as the purlin above it. STEM centre 1575, occupying 1525-1625, hard against the bar's inner face and turned the other way. The purlin line itself is at 1500 from the outer face, which is half the 3.0 m bearing run.
purlins._twoVerticals: A T IN PLAN, from two 50x100 of different heights, both standing on the tie - owner 2026-08-21. The BAR is short, sits directly under the purlin and bears. The STEM is long, sits beside the purlin turned PERPENDICULAR to it, runs past to the purlin top, and is screwed both to the purlin's face and to the bar. Looking down you see a T.
purlins._eachTurnedForItsOwnJob: This is the part worth not losing. The BAR is turned 100 mm ALONG the building because the purlin is only 50 wide, so only the along dimension buys seat area: 100 x 50 = 5000 mm2, 0.77 MPa, factor 2.2. Turned the other way it is 2500 and the factor halves to 1.1. The STEM is turned 100 mm ACROSS the building because roll restraint is a STIFFNESS job, not a strength one: as a cantilever off the tie it sways 2.1 mm this way against 8.4 mm turned parallel - four times stiffer for the same board, and the stresses are trivial either way (1.08 vs 2.15 MPa on a 50 N restraint force). Swap either piece and it gets worse at its own job.
purlins._stemStealsNothing: The stem is BESIDE the purlin, not under it, so it is not a second support: it adds no axial stiffness in the load path and steals no share from the strut. Only the bar bears. That separation is what lets each be optimised without compromising the other - and it is why the tie stays at 23.3 mm rather than the 26.5 a stiffer single post would cause.
purlins._verticals: 50x100 UNDER the purlin, standing on the tie, with a 100x100x100 HEAD BLOCK between it and the purlin. Owner 2026-08-21, and they were right to insist: the roof wants a direct bearing path down to the tie and the wall, not one that leans on the strut alone.
purlins._correctionSharedLoad: AN EARLIER NOTE HERE WAS WRONG and said a vertical under the purlin pushed the tie to 27.1 mm and failed. It used the strut's AXIAL force, 9.3 kN, as the load being shared. What gets shared is the purlin's REACTION - the vertical component - which at 47.8 deg is 6.89 kN. Redone: the vertical is stiffer than the strut (35.6 kN/mm against 29.0) so it takes 55%, 3.80 kN, and the tie goes 11.7 -> 23.1 mm against a 24 mm limit. IT PASSES. The strut then carries 3.10 kN vertical instead of 6.89, so its own head bearing improves from 1.38 to 0.62 MPa.
purlins._bolster: DROPPED 2026-08-21 at the owner's call - the T is two pieces, not three, and the bar bears the purlin directly. Kept here as a note because the option is real and the reasoning is worth keeping: a 50x100 laid FLAT on the bar, 300 mm long, It wins on BOTH checks for the same reason - laid flat it is crushed ACROSS its grain, so it is deliberately soft. BEARING: contact on the purlin underside goes from 100x50 to 300x50, 0.18 MPa against fc,90,d 1.73 - factor 9.6, up from 2.2. TIE: E90 is about E/30, so the bolster is 37 kN/mm in through-thickness compression; in series with the column's 38.1 that gives 18.8, the vertical's share of the purlin reaction falls 59% -> 39%, and the tie drops 23.8 -> 19.9 mm. Bolster onto the column head is 0.54 MPa, factor 3.2. On the lower derived reaction the tie is 16.9 mm.
purlins._softIsThePoint: If the bolster is ever revisited, this is why it worked: two supports under one purlin share by STIFFNESS, the bar lands mid-span on a tie and the strut lands over the wall, so every kN the bar sheds goes somewhere better. A soft layer is the mechanism, not a compromise - which is also why doubling the bar, or a full-height T, or a long stiff flange all make it worse. WITHOUT the bolster the numbers still pass: bar 5000 mm2, 0.77 MPa against 1.73 (factor 2.2), share 56%, tie 23.3 mm against 24.
purlins._widenTheHeadNotTheColumn: DOUBLING THE COLUMN to 100x100 is the wrong fix and makes things worse: stiffness doubles, its share goes 55% -> 71%, it takes 4.90 kN and the tie reaches 26.5 mm - over. Widen the HEAD instead. A 100x100 block on a 50x100 column gives 100 x 50 = 5000 mm2 of contact under the 50 wide purlin: 0.76 MPa against fc,90,d 1.73, factor 2.3, against 1.52 MPa and factor 1.1 for the bare head. The column's stiffness, and so its share, is untouched. Two 50x100 offcuts 100 mm long make each block - 3.2 m of byproduct for all 16.
purlins._rollRestraint: The purlin is 50x250 on edge, 5:1, and wants to roll. With the vertical back under it the head block and the rafter-spacer row that sits over the purlin do that job between them. If you want more, run ONE 50x100 up alongside the purlin to its top face at each frame and screw it to the purlin's side - that is the owner's two-different-heights sketch, and it adds restraint without adding anything to the load path.
purlins._reactionUncertainty: FLAGGED, not resolved. 6.89 kN comes from the schedule's 9.3 kN strut axial. A first-principles check off the roof loads - dead 0.15 kPa on slope, snow 0.141, wind 0.52, rafters at 700, purlin at mid-backspan - gives a frame reaction of 2.99 kN at SLS and 4.39 at ULS, a factor of 1.6 lower. The two cannot be reconciled from the notes alone. Everything above uses the CONSERVATIVE 6.89. If the lower figure is right, the tie lands nearer 19 mm than 23 and all of this has far more room.
purlins._doNotDouble: DO NOT double these to 100x100. It was considered on 2026-08-21 to widen a bearing seat, and it is the wrong move twice over: the vertical is not supposed to bear, and doubling makes it stiffer, so it steals MORE load from the strut and makes the tie worse.
purlins._strutBearsOn: Changed to 'tie' 2026-08-15 at owner's request. The struts and the purlin verticals now all sit ON the ties instead of dropping past them onto the wall plate, so the whole purlin frame sits in one plane. The old note - 'a post onto the tie adds 15 mm of sag to a beam already at its limit' - no longer applies: that was a post near MIDSPAN, and the ties were at 1151 mm deflecting 45.6 mm. The strut foot lands 25 mm inside the tie's bearing point, so it adds 0.36 mm. Tie goes 22.8 -> 23.2 mm against a 24 mm limit. Bearing on the tie top is 0.93 MPa against fc,90,d 1.73. The load drops straight through the tie depth into the plate - no bending path at all.
purlins._xBracing: OWNER 2026-08-21, and the reason is BUILDABILITY before it is stability. Each purlin frame is triangulated ACROSS the building - strut plus vertical make a triangle, collar ties the two sides. ALONG the building there is NOTHING: 8 frames joined only by two 50x250 purlins is a pinned parallelogram, and the rafters that would eventually stop it cannot go on until the purlins are already up. So this bracing was always going to exist; the only question was whether it was scrap that gets binned or a permanent member. Free either way off the rafter rip, so it stays in.
purlins._xBraceNumbers: CORRECTED 2026-08-21. The vertical is 1.565 m, not 1.815 - the purlin's full 250 mm depth sits ABOVE the post head, so postH = puTop - ud - tieTop. 7 bays per slope, frames 1.40 m apart: diagonal 2.10 m at 48.2 deg, NOT 2.29 at 52.4. Panel force is half the 12.9 kN gable triangle per purlin line, 6.45 kN, giving 9.67 kN in the diagonal. TENSION-ONLY ANYWAY: a 50x100 over 2.10 m has lambda 145 and kc 0.152, so 11.0 kN against 9.67 - it scrapes a factor of 1.14, which is not a number to hang a roof on. In tension the net section gives 38.8 kN, factor 4.0. Fit both diagonals of every X and let whichever is in tension do the work; the other goes slack and buckles harmlessly. CUT LENGTH 2.10 m - an earlier note in this file said 2.29 and would have had you cut 28 diagonals 190 mm long.
purlins._xBraceConnection: THE CONNECTION IS THE DESIGN, because tension bracing has no bearing to fall back on. 9.67 kN needs 7 x 6x120 per end - 28 diagonals x 2 ends is about 390 screws, and that is the real cost of this, not the timber.
purlins._xBracePromotes: It promotes two members. The VERTICALS go from 0.06 kN at a factor of 302 - genuinely throwaway - to 7.21 kN, factor 2.7 at 50x100 over 1.565 m. Still fine, but they now need real fixings top and bottom, not just locating. The PURLIN becomes the top chord at 6.4 kN axial, 0.52 MPa in a 50x250 - nothing.
purlins._xBraceDischarge: It has to land somewhere at both ends or it is a truss floating in the middle. The end frames sit at x = +-4.60 against the gable walls at +-4.65, so the end panels discharge straight into the gables - but that end connection has to be as real as the rest. Below, the X dumps into the ties, the ties into the wind girder (factor 10.3), the girder into the walls.
purlins._erectionSequence: BRACE EACH BAY BEFORE YOU LEAVE IT. 1. Ties bolted down first - 2 x M14 every end, permanent now (kneeBraces._endUplift), and you are standing on them. 2. Start at a gable: the end frame is held by the gable wall for free, and that is the anchor for the whole run. 3. Stand the next frame and fit its X back to the previous one IMMEDIATELY - never leave a frame standing on the purlin alone overnight. 4. The purlin FOLLOWS the frames; a 50x250 will not span 10.3 m of air waiting for supports. 5. Work in from one gable, or from both ends toward the middle. Until the second bay is braced a single braced bay carries everything - fine for erection wind, but do not leave it part-braced with weather coming.
purlins._cutShortPieceFirst: TWO BOARDS PER RUN, 5.30 + 6.00, AND THE ORDER MATTERS. 11.30 m from 6 m stock is obviously two boards with 0.70 m off - the owner is right and an earlier 3-piece scheme here was over-cautious, costing a board AND adding two more joints. What the earlier scheme was chasing was a joint over a support, and cutting in the right order gets that for free: run the 5.30 piece from the FRONT and the joint lands at -0.35, which is 50 mm from the purlin frame at -0.40 and 25 mm from the rafter at -0.325. Cut 6.00 first instead and the same joint lands at +0.35 - 650 mm from the nearest frame, out in the middle of a bay. Same two boards, same waste, and the difference is which end you start from. ALL THREE RUNS use the same cut, so 3 x 2 = 6 boards, exactly the six uncut in the yard.
purlins._splice: THREE PIECES, 3.85 + 4.90 + 2.55, splicing on the frames at -1.80 and +3.10. At an 11.30 m run NO single splice can land on a frame with both pieces under 6 m - that needs a frame within 0.35 m of centre and the nearest is at -0.40 - so the two-piece solution below is dead. Both end pieces run past the gable and carry the 1.05 m verge cantilever unspliced, which is the part that matters. SUPERSEDED NOTE: 4.75 + 5.55, NOT the 6.00 + 4.30 the cut list had. 6.00 + 4.30 puts the joint at x = +0.85 and the nearest frame is at +1.00 - a 50x250 lap hanging 150 mm off its support. 4.75 + 5.55 lands it exactly on the frame at -0.40. Same two boards, both inside 6 m stock, no extra material; it is only which end you cut from. It is also the ONLY option: for a splice to reach a frame with both pieces under 6 m the frame must sit within +-0.85 m of centre, and -0.40 is the only one that does. Both purlin runs splice there - they are 3 m apart across the building, so the joints are not adjacent.
purlins.jointType: bears on a 100x100 head block, located by a 10 mm housing, purlin uncut
purlins._rabbet: Owner 2026-08-16: rabbet joint at the purlin/post 90 deg connection. CUT THE POST, NOT THE PURLIN. A rebate on the underside of a beam at a support is the one case EN 1995 6.5.2 singles out - the re-entrant corner starts a shear crack along the grain and it runs. Numbers for a 50x250 purlin at V=4.65 kN: uncut 23.1 kN (factor 5.0), 25 mm rebate 19.6 (4.2), 50 mm 13.0 (2.8), 75 mm 9.8 (2.1). It does not fail on numbers, but three things do not show in that check: the purlin is CONTINUOUS so the notch sits where hogging moment and peak shear coincide and kv is optimistic; the purlin is only 50 mm wide so the corner splits easily when the fixing is driven; and the post head is in pure compression where a housing costs bearing area and nothing else.
purlins._housingDepth: 10 mm, LOCATING ONLY - not the 30 mm structural housing this used to be. The purlin sits in a shallow recess in the head block so it cannot walk sideways; it still bears on the full 100 x 50 at the bottom of the recess, so the depth costs no area. The old note here analysed 25/40/50 mm housings into a post head on the premise of a 100 x 100 contact - 0.93 MPa at 9.3 kN implies 10,000 mm2, and the purlin is only 50 WIDE. That premise was 2x optimistic and is gone. SAME RULE AS THE KNEE BRACE: shallow to locate, never a deep notch into a member carrying something else.
purlins._cutBothHeadsSquare: The vertical's block and the strut's head both bear under the purlin, sharing 55/45. Each has to be CUT SQUARE and actually touch: a head that bears in two places has no factor at all, and with two supports a sloppy one just hands its share to the other. The strut head is the harder cut because it arrives at 47.8 deg - mark it off the erected frame, not off a drawing.
purlins._ifYouRebatePurlin: If the purlin is rebated anyway: 25 mm maximum (10% of depth); do NOT square the internal corner - drill it to an 8-10 mm radius or taper the cut, because a square re-entrant corner is the crack starter and that is the entire failure mode; keep fixings at least 50 mm clear of the corner.

loft.src: given — 50 mm floor over the 250 mm tie beams, 2.2 m walking height wanted in the middle bay between the rafter supports
loft._thickness: 40 mm. The old note here was written for the 1.06 m clear span of the 1151 mm setout - 1.0 mm final against a 3.5 mm limit, 3.7 MPa under a 1.5 kN point load. At 600 mm centres on 100 mm ties the clear span is 500 mm and the deck is nowhere: 0.05 mm and 1.8 MPa. 32 mm was the calculated minimum; 40 buys real margin for machinery and costs 137 EUR over it.
loft._sheetModule: 700 mm centres do NOT suit 1200 mm sheet - 1200 is not a multiple of 700, so a sheet edge lands on a tie only every 6th bay (4200 mm). The insulation module won this argument over the sheet module. Consequences, both real: cut sheet edges have to be supported on noggins where they fall between ties, and 18 mm OSB is no longer enough. See _deckThickness.
loft._deckThickness: 22 mm OSB, NOT 18. 18 mm OSB/3 is rated to 600 mm CENTRES; at 700 mm centres it is outside the span tables. The 40 mm boarding in loft.floorThickness carries 600 mm clear easily (0.10 mm) and is the fallback if boards are preferred to sheet. Do not buy 18 mm for this floor.
loft._stairBaySpan: CHECKED 2026-08-21: there is no soft span in the stair bay. The only decked part of it is y +1.0 to +3.0 - everything from the wall at y -3.0 up to the trimmer at +1.0 is the opening - and the tail joist on the setout station at +3.80 splits that 1.40 m bay into 600 and 800 mm centres, 500 and 700 mm clear. 40 mm boarding over 700 is 0.2 mm and 2.4 MPa. Nothing to do.

site.src: location given by paperwork; loads are EN 1991 Latvian NA typical values, to be confirmed

blocking.fixing: screwed through the tie from both faces; staggered so opposing screws miss each other
blocking.src: given - 3 rows of 50 mm spacer blocks between the ties, screwed from both sides
blocking._depth: 50x100, dropped from full 250 depth 2026-08-15. The tie does not need lateral restraint at all - 100x250 over 6 m has lambda,rel 0.749 and kcrit 1.00, it is too stocky for LTB. The blocking is there to hold the ties upright BEFORE the deck goes on, and to give a nailing edge where OSB sheets butt. Both jobs are at the TOP of the tie, so it sits flush with the top face. Free from the rip byproduct; saves 4 boards of 50x250.

braces._note: As built. Front gable has 3 because bracing there is unfinished - it wants a 4th.
braces.geometry: foot of a post up to the girt, within an end bay
braces._upper: NOT DRAWN. Owner is supplying and detailing the girt-to-corner wall braces from separate material, so they are out of both the model and the take-off - keeping them in only invited them to be confused with the new order. The capability is still here: set upperPlanned true to draw them again at braces.upperSection.
braces._upperSection: 50x100 nominal. OWNER SUPPLIES SEPARATELY - removed from the take-off 2026-08-16 so it does not mix with the new material order. It previously drew 22.1 m off the rafter-rip byproduct; that is now free, taking the 50x100 spare from 82 m to 104 m. The order does not change either way, because these were never bought.

advice._cornerBrace: OWNER 2026-08-21: 45 deg diagonals across each corner, in plan, in a plane just under the wind girder. Four off, 50x100, 1.131 m long, free from the rafter rip. What they buy: the plan rectangle goes rigid at the corner, and - the real reason - the wind girder gets somewhere to land. Each girder diagonal delivers 12.57 kN into a corner that is otherwise a lap joint between two hewn plates. A 50x100 at 1.131 m carries 33.8 kN in compression (lambda 78, kc 0.465) and 38.8 in tension, so factor 2.7 even if one takes the whole girder force.
advice._cornerBraceRun: 0.8 m, NOT 1.0 - and this is a clash, not a preference. The tie sits in the z band 3.410-3.510, tucked under the girder. The KNEE BRACES sweep through y 2.526-2.626 in that same band. At a 1.0 m run the dragon tie crosses the second tie line at y = 2.600, which is inside that sweep: a hard clash with the knee brace at x = 3.90. At 0.8 m it crosses at y = 2.800 and clears by 174 mm. 0.6 m clears by 226 mm and 1.2 m by 126 mm, so if you want it longer, 1.2 works and 1.0 does not - the clash is a window, not a threshold.
advice._legend: YELLOW = must. WHITE = required by the all-directions wind check. Orange precautions dropped 2026-08-14 - roof-plane bracing became mandatory (white), the extra purlin struts were superseded by the two-panel X, and the verge outriggers were declined.
advice._girder: 100x100, BOUGHT - changed 2026-08-15 at owner's request so the girder no longer eats 100x250. It works only because the ties are close: the girder is screwed to every tie it crosses, which at 600 mm in x is a restraint every 955 mm along the diagonal. lambda 33.1, kc 0.93, capacity about 135 kN against a 7.1 kN demand. At the old 1151 mm tie spacing the restraint was 1834 mm, kc 0.633 - which is why the schedule previously insisted on 100x125. Going 576 -> 600 mm changes nothing here. Fixing to EVERY crossing is not optional.
advice._gableStud: 100x100. NOT an axial check - the stud spans 3.54 m carrying wind pressure on the gable, so bending governs. At 50x100 the combined ratio is 1.03 and deflection 25.0 mm against an L/200 limit of 17.7 mm; both fail. 100x100 gives 0.37 and 12.5 mm. It also cannot be ripped from 100x250 any more - the 17-tie run consumes every 100x250 on site.
advice._white: Required by the all-directions wind check. Gable studs frame the triangle above the eaves; roof-plane diagonals carry its 12.9 kN along the roof into the walls. 100x100 - a 100x50 diagonal buckles at 2.4 kN against 7.17.
advice._maxLength: Longest available piece is 6.0 m. The wind girder was 6.73 m over 3 tie bays; at 1 bay it is 5.83 m, fits, and carries LESS force (6.14 vs 7.08 kN) because the diagonal is steeper. Plates, purlins and ridge all exceed 6 m and must be spliced - see docs/findings.md F16.
advice.spliceScrews: 4 x 6x200 each side of every joint, spread over ~600 mm, staggered
advice.windGirderLayout: two-panel X - each diagonal gable corner to mid-wall, 7.36 m, 4 off
advice._roofBracing: Owner decision 2026-08-14: the 4 corner-to-ridge roof-plane braces are NOT being fitted. The 12.9 kN gable-triangle load then relies entirely on the metal roof sheeting acting as a diaphragm. See F19.
advice._builtUp: Two 50x100 screwed face to face is NOT a 100x100. EN 1995 Annex B/C: the joint slips, so gamma is 0.06-0.15 over these short lengths and the effective second moment of area is a quarter of solid. At 2.19 m it gives 24-27 kN against 71 kN solid. Still passes the 9.3 kN strut demand at a factor of 2.6-2.9, so it is a valid FALLBACK if 100x100 is not available in 6 m - but it costs more in ripped 50x250 than buying 100x100 and doubles the screwing. Screws at 100 mm, not 200.

tieToWall.detail: galvanised angle bracket each side of the tie, screwed; 45 deg knee brace below as the second path
tieToWall.src: owner 2026-08-15 - through-bolting 700 mm of tie plus wall is not realistic
tieToWall._supersedes: Replaces the 2 x M14 through-rod detail. That needed a 700 mm hole through the 250 mm tie and 450 mm of wall top; the owner's drill reaches 800 mm but the hole is not a realistic site operation.
tieToWall._capacity: Demand 3.13 kN horizontal and 0.92 kN uplift per tie end. A 5x40 connector screw through thin steel gives 0.98 kN design (EN 1995 8.2.3, mode a governs). 6 per leg x 2 brackets = 11.8 kN, factor 3.8. The angle steel itself rates 5-8 kN for a 2.5 mm 90x90, so the pair is 10-12 kN whichever way it is counted.
tieToWall._secondPath: The 45 deg knee braces give the horizontal force an independent route - tie to brace to ledger to POSTS, 424 mm below the tie underside and 84 mm below the plate courses - taking most of the 1.96 kN thrust component off the bracket, and keeping it off the lapped plate (F16) altogether. Neither detail is relied on alone, which is what you want in a joint that cannot be inspected once the loft is decked.
tieToWall._notTheNotch: Do NOT count the 50 mm housing as restraint. The tie runs out to the wall face and on into the building, so the trench is open at both ends along the tie axis. It locates the tie sideways and carries it vertically; it resists nothing along its length.
tieToWall._workmanship: 1. Z275 HOT-DIP galvanised, not electroplated - unheated building, Baltic winter, condensation off a metal roof. 2. Manufacturer's hardened connector screws, NOT drywall screws: drywall screws are brittle in shear and this is a pure shear connection, they snap without warning. 3. FILL EVERY HOLE in both legs - the rating assumes it, and a part-filled bracket is an eccentric joint that peels rather than a weaker one. 4. BOTH sides, or the tie rotates about the single bracket and pries the screws out. 5. Knee brace screws SKEWED, 2 into the face and 2 angled - four square screws let the joint hinge, and a hinged knee brace does nothing.

advice._gableStudSpacing: 600 mm (588 actual), changed from 800 on 2026-08-15. NOT a strength fix - 800 already passed at combined ratio 0.36 and 12.2 mm deflection. The reason is the CLADDING GRID: gable battens sit on the studs, so at 800 the sheet would land on 600 mm spacing up the wall and 800 across the gable. 600 makes it one grid top to bottom. Costs 10.3 m more 100x100, 2 boards, EUR 37. At 588 mm the tallest stud is now 4.08 m (a stud lands at the centre, where there was none before): combined 0.38, 16.2 mm against an L/200 limit of 20.4 mm.
advice._gablePanelSection: 50x250, matching the 2 boards in the take-off. The model drew these at 160x60, a section that appears nowhere in the order. Caught in the same audit.
advice._gableStudBearsOn: Owner 2026-08-16: the gable studs stand on the END TIE, not on the wall plate. The tie sits at x = +-4.605 and the gable wall at +-4.655, so they are parallel and 50 mm apart for the tie's whole length. Each stud gets 200 mm shorter - tallest 4.08 -> 3.88 m - which improves it: bending 5.14 -> 4.64 MPa, deflection 16.2 -> 13.2 mm against an L/200 limit of 19.4. 18 studs x 200 mm = 3.6 m less 100x100.
advice._gableStudCondition: CORRECTED 2026-08-16. I raised a 79 mm deflection concern by treating the end tie as free-spanning between the long walls like the other 14. It is not. The end tie occupies x 4.555-4.655 and the gable wall 4.505-4.655: the tie's FULL 100 mm width sits over the gable wall, notched 50 mm into its plate, for the whole 6 m. It is continuously supported, so the studs' horizontal reaction goes straight down into the gable wall exactly as it did when they bore on the plate. There is no free-span weak-axis case and the 79 mm never existed.
advice._gableStudFixing: Still fix the end tie down to the gable plate - not for the bending that does not happen, but because the studs deliver a horizontal push at the tie top and the tie has to be held against sliding and lifting. The 2 x M14 already scheduled at every tie end cover the ends; add fixings along the length at each gable post.

plateSplices._note: Top plate is not continuous - lower layer 2 pieces, upper 4. The joints are LAP joints with M14 through, and the two courses are bolted to each other with M14 as well. Corrected 2026-08-15: the model previously assumed BUTT joints, which was the basis of F16 as a critical finding.
plateSplices._recut: Piece lengths restated for the 10.30 m run (9.30 m building + 0.50 m verge each end). The SPLICE POSITIONS are as-built and do not move - lower at -0.65, upper at -1.65, +1.35, +3.35 - because the cut comes off the ends, not the middle. F16a is WORSE under the 600 mm tie setout, not better: J6 at -1.60 and J11 at +1.40 now sit 50 mm from an upper-layer splice, against 72 and 79 mm before. See joists._spliceClash.
plateSplices._capacity: Chord demand is 4.46 kN - the along-span component of the 7.1 kN wind-girder diagonal. One M14 in the lap gives 7.1 kN (factor 1.6), two give 14.2 kN (factor 3.2). A butt joint gives zero, which is why F16 was critical. EN 1995 spacing for M14 parallel to grain: a1 = 5d = 70 mm bolt to bolt, a3,t = 7d = 98 mm to a loaded end, a4 = 3d = 42 mm to the edge. Two bolts each side needs 266 mm of lap; 300 mm is specified. The 150 mm plate width allows ONE bolt line only.
plateSplices._composite: Bolting the two 150x185 courses together turns them into a 150x370 section: I goes from 158 to 633 x10^-6 m4, four times stiffer, if the bolts stop slip. Even partial composite action is a large gain and is exactly what F16 asked for.

cladding.spec: Dekorativo delu apsuvums per the permit; 22 mm boarding
cladding._note: Walls 105.3 m2 + gable triangles 29.1 m2 = 134.5 m2, 2.96 m3, ~918 EUR. Not yet ordered.

rafterSpacers._why: NOT for lateral-torsional buckling - kcrit is 0.99 at 50x150, the rafter does not need it. Three other reasons: (a) EN 1995 wants the rafter held upright where it bears on the plate and on the purlin; (b) F19 deleted the roof-plane braces, so the 12.9 kN gable triangle now relies on the sheeting acting as a diaphragm, and sheeting cannot do that unless the rafters are tied to one another; (c) they hold the 600 mm setout while you work. No ridge row - the rafters are screwed to the ridge purlin, which already does it.
rafterSpacers._qty: 2 rows x 17 bays x 2 slopes = 68 spacers, 550 mm long in the 600 mm bays, cut from rafter offcuts.
rafterSpacers._section: 50x100, free. Ripping 42 rafters from 50x250 down to 50x150 throws off 252 m of 50x100; the 80 spacers need 42 m of it. They are not bending members - they hold the rafters upright and tie them together - so 100 deep is ample.

stair._which: The CLOSE-OUT BAY at the back, between the tie at +3.20 and the end tie at +4.60. The station at +3.80 is set out but carries no tie - only the rafter beside it and the tail joist that closes the deck past the opening. The end tie sits at +4.60 and the gable wall at +4.65, so the opening's far edge IS the end wall: the stair runs tight against it and the middle of the loft floor stays clear. Owner decision 2026-08-15, re-set out on the 600 mm grid 2026-08-21.
stair._openingWidth: 1.30 m clear, 1.40 m centre to centre. Was 1.051 m. It got wider for free: the 200 mm that 9.20 m leaves over after thirteen 600 mm bays lands here. Owner asked for 1.20 m minimum for the stair - this beats it by 100 mm.
stair._fromThe14thTie: OWNER 2026-08-21 has 14 ties placed, one at every setout station INCLUDING 8450 - the one the model omits for the stair. It cannot stay: with it in, the two gaps are 600 and 700 mm clear and the 900 mm flight passes through neither. And the reason offered for keeping it does not hold - the tie flanking the stair is the LEAST loaded tie in the building, not the most, at 9.6 mm final against 11.7 for a typical one, because it loses the deck over four of its six metres. There is no pressure there to reduce. BUT DO NOT PULL IT OUT WHOLE. Cut it at y = +1.0: the outer 2.0 m is already notched into the wall at y = +3.0 and IS the tail joist, in 100x250 instead of a bought 50x150, with no handling at all. The 4 m offcut yields the 1.50 m trimmer in the same section. Everything then sits flush top and bottom with the ties, which removes the depth mismatch the 50x150 pair had, and it takes the stairOpening board out of the order.
stair._trimmerHeadroom: The deeper trimmer costs 100 mm of headroom at the head of the stair - its underside drops from tie-top-less-150 to the tie underside. 2.51 m becomes 2.41 m over the top tread. Still comfortable; noted because the stair tops out at y = +1.0, which is exactly where this member sits.
stair._headroom: The binding constraint is NOT the opening, it is loft headroom. Full standing height exists only within +/-1.23 m of the centre (2.20 m at 1.23 m, 1.82 m at 1.50 m), so the stair has to EMERGE near the middle. Running from the wall at y=-3.0 to y=+1.0 gives a 4.00 m run over a 3.68 m rise: 21 risers at 175 mm, 200 mm going, 42.6 deg. Steep - a domestic stair wants 220 going - but this is a workshop.
stair._opening: Only 2.0 m of opening is needed, not the whole 4.0 m run. The loft floor only blocks your head once you are above 1.88 m of climb, which is the top 49% of the run. The rest of the bay is closed by a tail joist from the trimmer to the wall.
stair._structure: Tail joist 1.9 m delivers 1.09 kN to the trimmer; the trimmer spans 1.151 m between J14 and J16 at 1.7 MPa against 14.8. The rafter at J15 loses its tie, so its 0.98 kN thrust goes into the plate instead - plate bending about the vertical axis is 0.41 MPa. Both negligible.
stair._tailJoist: 50x150, not 100x250 - changed 2026-08-15. Over its 1.9 m span it runs 2.77 MPa against 14.8 and deflects 2.3 mm final against a 7.6 mm limit. It is a FLOOR JOIST, not a rafter tie: the tie at J15 is gone entirely and that rafter's thrust already goes into the plate. Trimmer and tail joist together are 3.05 m, so both come out of one ripped 50x250 - which removes 100x250 from the order completely.

flight._status: SHOWN IN RED, NOT IN THE TAKE-OFF. It bears on a concrete floor that is not poured yet - that comes after the roof is on. Drawn only to check it clears the opening and the rafters. stock.js does not know about it.
flight._geometry: 20 risers at 185 mm over the 3.700 m rise, 265 going. LOWER flight 7 risers running +x from x 1.76 to the landing at 3.35, against the -y wall. LANDING 900 x 900 at 1.495 m. UPPER flight 13 risers running +y from -1.95 to +1.23, in the omitted-tie gap at x 3.35-4.25.
flight._strings: 50x150 HOUSED, and the mid-flight newel is now MANDATORY, not optional. A cut string is impossible at 150: notching for a 175 mm rise removes 132 mm, leaving 18 mm. Housed keeps the depth but takes the thickness from 50 to ~35 at each housing. Over the full 5.44 m that gives 29.6 MPa and 110 mm of deflection against an 18.1 mm limit - it FAILS. With one newel the span halves: 7.4 MPa and 6.9 mm against 9.1 mm. Passes, but the margin is modest, so the newel is structural, not a handrail post.
flight._pitchCorrected: 42.6 deg, not the 41.2 recorded until 2026-08-21. The old figure divided the rise by 21 GOINGS (4.20 m) when 21 risers give 20 goings and a 4.00 m run - which is also the run the flight actually occupies, y = -3.0 to +1.0. The string length 5.44 was always computed off 4.00 and was right; only the angle was wrong. It matters because steepness is already the open decision here: the stair is 1.4 deg steeper than the notes said.
flight._decideBeforeSlab: 42.6 deg at a 200 mm going is steep - domestic wants 220+. This CANNOT be fixed later: the run is fixed by loft headroom (you must emerge within 1.23 m of the centre) and by the 6 m width. A 220 going needs 4.40 m of run, 0.40 m more than exists, which means a winder or a half-landing - and a landing has to be set out in the slab. Decide before the concrete goes down.
flight._material: 2 strings x 5.44 m of 50x250 (2 boards), 20 treads x 0.90 m of 40x250 (3 boards), 1 newel 1.9 m of 100x100. About 0.33 m3, EUR 102. NOT in the current order - it waits for the slab, which waits for the roof.
flight._treads: 50x250, NOT 50x150. Strength was never the issue - 50 thick over the 900 mm between strings is 5.4 MPa and 1.33 mm under a 1.5 kN point load. DEPTH is: the going is 200 mm, so a 150 board leaves a 50 mm GAP between consecutive treads and drops the effective going to 150. Open risers need treads to OVERLAP by at least 16 mm. 250 gives 50 mm of overlap. Taken free from the 4 spare 50x250 (18 m needed, 24 m available). QUARTER-TURN: 18 treads, still two 50x150 per tread for the 100 mm overlap, so 36 pieces at 0.90 m.
flight._deferred: DEFERRED 2026-08-16. Strings, treads and newel are out of this order. They wait on the slab, which waits on the roof, so nothing is held up - and buying them now left 50x250 at 50 of 50 with zero margin on the section that matters most. Deferring restores 4 spare boards. When it comes: 2 x 50x150 strings (5.44 m), 20 x 50x250 treads (0.90 m, 6 per board = 4 boards), 1 x 100x100 newel (1.90 m). About EUR 150 at 2026 prices.
flight._openingStays: The stair OPENING is NOT deferred. The trimmer spans between J15 and J17 and the tail joist runs back to the wall - both have to be framed when the ties go in, or you are cutting into a finished loft floor later.
flight._allOneSection: Owner 2026-08-16: build the whole stair from 50x150 and put it back in the order. Works, and it comes out EUR 14 CHEAPER than the mixed-section version (125.55 against 139.50) because 0.90 m tread pieces nest 6 to a board while 50x250 treads waste a third of every board. One section instead of three.
flight._treadsDoubled: TWO 50x150 per tread, butted - 300 mm deep. A SINGLE 150 board does not work: the going is 200 mm, so one board leaves a 50 mm GAP between consecutive treads and drops the effective going to 150. Open risers need treads to OVERLAP by at least 16 mm. Doubled gives 100 mm of overlap. 40 pieces for 20 treads.
flight._newel150: 50x150 newel carries it: the strings' mid-span reaction is about 7.1 kN and even on the weak axis (lambda 127.5, kc 0.195) capacity is 21.2 kN, factor 3.0. 100x100 would give 12.9 but needs a section bought for one 1.84 m piece.
flight._landingIsOversize: The landing is 1.125 m in x, not 900. Flight 1 needs only 5 goings = 1.325 m of its 1.55 m of available run, so the 225 mm left over goes into the landing rather than being lost. A bigger landing at a turn is never wrong, and it is below the loft so it costs no opening.
flight._supersededStraight: SUPERSEDED 2026-08-24 by the quarter-turn. STAYS STRAIGHT. A turn was considered and rejected: the scarce dimension is the 6 m width, and a landing eats the same 3.85 m the flight needs. Every landing variant came out at 170-209 mm going against 196 mm straight - no better, mostly worse. And a turn is precisely what stops you carrying sheets: a 2.5 m board can round a right angle between 1.2 m widths only ON EDGE, which needs 2.5 m of headroom, and a mid-height landing has 2.04 m under the loft floor. Straight is better for both the pitch and the boards.
flight._newels: TWO. One at the TURN carrying the landing corner. One MID-FLIGHT on the upper run, because a housed 50x150 string over its 4.07 m still deflects about 34 mm against a 13.6 mm limit. The LOWER flight needs none - its string is 2.13 m and comes out near 2 mm.
flight._stringLengths: lower 2.13 m x 2, upper 4.07 m x 2 - against a single 5.44 m pair on the straight version.

stair._widened: REVERTED to one omitted tie. I had sized the opening at 1627 mm on the premise that a 1200 x 2500 board has to pass through horizontally. It does not - carried ON EDGE, 1200 vertical and the long axis up the slope, the board's plan footprint is its THICKNESS. It needs about 250 mm of width including hands, against 1051 mm available. What actually has to fit is the LENGTH: 2500 tilted at 42.6 deg projects 1881 mm against a 2.0 m opening, 119 mm spare. Owner confirmed they carry board vertically.
stair._trimmer: 50x150 over the widened 1.727 m span carrying two tail joists: 3.5 MPa, 0.6 mm.

baseSupport._bearing: No separate foundation needed. 5.6 kN reaches the bottom, 2.8 kN per string. Bearing the 50x250 string end directly is 447 kPa and will craze and dish a 70 mm slab. A 100 x 1200 SOLE PLATE drops it to 47 kPa, against roughly 100-150 kPa locally available. Costs one offcut.
baseSupport._slabPrep: BLIND THE STONE before pouring - 25-50 mm of sand or crushed fines, compacted. 50-200 mm stone has huge voids and 70 mm of concrete poured straight onto it loses half its depth into the gaps with the mesh ending up on the stone. Compact in 200 mm lifts. Mesh on chairs in the middle of the slab. 70 mm is below the usual 100 mm for a ground slab - fine for the stair, marginal for a workshop floor, so thicken to 150 mm under the stair base and wherever a machine will stand.
baseSupport._movement: DO NOT BOLT THE BOTTOM DOWN. The stair top is fixed to the trimmer, which sits on ties on 1.2 m piles; the bottom sits on a slab at grade. Same split as F23 - the slab heaves seasonally, the piles do not, and a stair fixed rigidly at both ends racks every winter. Fix the top properly and let the bottom simply BEAR on a sole plate over a DPC, located against sideways movement only.

stair._topPosition: The flight can START anywhere; where it ENDS is fixed by the roof. Headroom over the top tread: 2.51 m at y=1.0, 2.20 m at y=1.23, 1.82 m at y=1.5, 1.14 m at y=2.0. Top out beyond 1.23 m from the centre and you hit the roof standing on the last tread. That is geometry from the 54 deg pitch and the 3.88 m floor, not a preference - so the stair tops out at y=+1.0 and cannot be pushed further toward the long wall.
stair._quarterTurn: QUARTER-TURN, owner 2026-08-24. The stair still SURFACES WHERE IT ALWAYS DID - the back bay, station 13 omitted, emerging at y +1.23. Only the APPROACH moved: instead of the whole run coming off the -y wall across the width, the lower flight now runs ALONG the building toward the back and turns 90 deg LEFT onto the upper flight. You face the back as you climb, then turn to face the centre.
stair._whyItIsBetter: The straight stair had to find its whole 4.00 m run inside the 6 m width, and lost: 21 risers at 176 mm with a 200 going, 41.2 deg, 2R+G 552 - a going 20 mm under domestic minimum. The turn lets the LOWER flight borrow run from the 9.30 m length, which the straight version never touched. 20 risers at 185, 265 going, 34.9 deg, 2R+G 635 - inside the 600-660 band. The going grows 65 mm and the pitch drops 6.3 degrees, for no extra floor area that was doing anything else.
stair._theThreeConstraints: (1) THE LOWER FLIGHT CROSSES THE TIES, so its ceiling is the tie underside at 3.610, not the deck at 3.860. The landing must sit at or below 1.610 for 2.0 m of headroom, which caps the lower flight at 7 risers - it lands at 1.495, with 115 mm to spare. 21 risers would put it at exactly 1.610 and was rejected for that. (2) THE UPPER FLIGHT RUNS BETWEEN TIES, parallel to them, so it has to fit the 1.40 m clear that omitting station 13 leaves: 900 wide at x 3.35-4.25, 250 mm each side. (3) YOU MUST EMERGE WITHIN 1.23 m OF THE CENTRE or the roof is on your head. The upper flight tops out at exactly +1.23, headroom 2.18 m. All three are geometry, not preference.
stair._openingIsBigger: 2.385 m of opening against 2.0 m before, and it needs TWO trimmers rather than one, because the hole is now in the middle of a bay instead of hard against the gable. Opening runs y -1.155 to +1.23: below -1.155 you are still under the deck with 2.0 m clear, so the tie stub and the deck stay. Trimmers span the 1.40 m between the ties at -3.20 and -1.80.
stair._openingGrew: y -1.42 to +1.23, 2.65 m, and TWO trimmers instead of one - the hole is in the middle of a bay now, bounded at both ends. Below -1.42 you are still under the deck with 2.0 m clear, so the tie stub and the decking stay. Trimmers span the 1.50 m between the ties at +3.10 and +4.60.

slab.dpm: 0.3 mm (1200 gauge) polythene; 0.5 mm (2000 gauge) better for a workshop
slab.src: owner 2026-08-16 - concrete floor, steel reinforcement, leftover rock and brick as fill
slab._levels: Slab top at 250 mm - 50 ABOVE the sill underside (200), at the owner's request 2026-08-16. Superseded the earlier 150 mm. This only works because the slab STOPS AT THE WALL INNER FACE: the 150 mm wide strip under the sill, from grade to 200 mm, stays open to outside between the piles. Run the slab to the outer face instead and it buries the sill's bottom 50 mm and seals the drying void completely - the two requirements would then contradict.
slab._fourJobs: The single move of finishing at 150 does four things: the slab never touches timber; the void vents inside-to-outside all round; there is no capillary path because there is no contact; and the slab can shrink and heave without levering the frame (F23).
slab._perimeterGap: 20 mm horizontal at the slab edge with a compressible closed-cell strip. That is a MOVEMENT joint, not a moisture one - concrete shrinks ~0.5 mm/m, so 9.31 m of slab moves 4.7 mm before thermal. The moisture job is done by the air gap above it.
slab._thickness: 125 mm MINIMUM, 150 RECOMMENDED. Judged on CORNER loading, not interior: a slab is weakest at a free corner and the entrance is exactly that. Under a 10 kN machine foot, C25/30 allowable 1.73 MPa - 70 mm gives 2.63 MPa at a corner and fails; 100 mm gives 1.54, passing with almost nothing spare; 125 gives 1.08; 150 gives 0.79. Punching is never critical (57-124 kN against 10). Thicken to 200 mm for 1.5 m in from the entrance - free corner AND every wheel load.
slab._dpm: THE FILM UNDER THE SLAB - already in this spec from the start, and it is the primary moisture barrier. 1200 gauge (0.3 mm) minimum; 2000 gauge (0.5 mm) is worth the small extra on a workshop where you will drop things on it before the pour. Lap 300 mm and TAPE every lap - an untaped lap is not a barrier. Turn it UP at the perimeter, behind the foam, to slab top level. It also blocks the sulfates in the brick hardcore from reaching the cement, and doubles as a basic radon barrier if the laps are properly sealed.
slab._hardcore: Owner's leftover rock and brick. CLEAN brick and stone only - no plaster, gypsum, plasterboard, wood or soil. Gypsum is the worst sulfate source there is. Compact in 150 mm lifts, not one dumped layer. BLIND IT with 50 mm of sand or crushed fines: 50-200 mm rock has huge voids and concrete poured straight onto it loses depth into the gaps.
slab._mesh: Owner has the steel — NOT bought. 2026-08-16. Target is A252: 252 mm2 per metre EACH WAY. Anything meeting that works: 8 mm @ 200 (this IS A252), 6 @ 100, 8 @ 150, 10 @ 250 or 300, 12 @ 400. Saves about EUR 210 ex VAT, the biggest non-concrete line in the floor.
slab._quantities: 150 mm over 55.9 m2 with the entrance thickened = 8.6 m3 concrete. Hardcore 8.4 m3 (owner's). Blinding 2.8 m3 (buy). DPM 64 m2. Mesh 61 m2.
slab._doors: Doors are automatic and hang off the wall and ties, so they put almost nothing on the floor. The entrance thickening is for wheel and foot traffic and the free corner, not the door.
slab._whyAbove: A workshop floor gets hosed and water finds the lowest edge. At 150 the floor sat BELOW the timber, so standing water pooled against the sill line. At 250 it drains away from the wall. The owner's instinct is right; it just moves the burden onto the edge joint.
slab._edgeDetail: THREE things become mandatory once the slab edge sits BESIDE the sill rather than below it. (1) VERTICAL DPC at the slab edge, turned up the full 50 mm and over the top - a 20 mm air gap alone is not enough when the faces are level with each other. (2) SEAL THE TOP of the joint with flexible sealant over the compressible filler, or floor water runs into the slot and down into the void you are keeping dry. (3) EDGE RETENTION: there is now a 350 mm vertical face of hardcore and slab with open void beyond, and it will spill - permanent formwork, a kerb, or batter the hardcore back.
slab._dig: Raising the floor 100 mm halves the excavation: 200 mm becomes 100 mm, about 5.6 m3 less spoil off a 55.9 m2 footprint. Build-up unchanged: slab 150 (100-250), blinding 50 (50-100), hardcore 150 (-100 to 50), formation at -100.
slab._dpmPuncture: The DPM is why the 50 mm blinding is not optional. Laid straight onto 50-200 mm rock it gets punctured in a dozen places by the first person who walks on it, and a punctured membrane is no membrane. It sits on sand or crushed fines, never on the stone.
slab._foam: Owner 2026-08-16: XPS foam in the perimeter gap so slab and sill never touch. Correct on the main point - no contact means no capillary bridge. Three qualifications. (1) Use XPS, not EPS: closed cell, under 0.7% water absorption against 2-5% for EPS, and on a 20 mm strip the price difference is pennies. (2) Foam is NOT a DPC - vapour crosses it much as it crosses air, and unlike an air gap it HOLDS water that gets in. (3) The joint must DRAIN: it is only 50 mm tall before it breaks out into the ventilated strip under the sill at 200 mm, so seal the TOP with flexible sealant against hose water and swarf, and leave the BOTTOM open. Run the foam past 200 mm and the joint becomes a reservoir.
slab._foamRealJob: What the foam is actually earning its place for is MOVEMENT, not moisture. The slab shrinks 4.7 mm over 9.31 m and heaves seasonally while the piles do not (F23). A rigid fill there would lever the frame; foam absorbs it.
slab._vehicleLoads: CHECKED 2026-08-16: yes, the slab takes a car easily. Westergaard on 150 mm C25/30, allowable 1.73 MPa (plain-concrete basis, conservative - the A252 only helps after cracking). Worst case is always the free CORNER, which is where you drive in: 2000 kg car (5 kN wheel) 0.38 MPa, factor 4.6; loaded 3500 kg van (10 kN) 0.75 MPa, factor 2.3; 20 kN truck axle 1.50 MPa, still inside. Only a 40 kN mixer wheel goes over at a corner, and that is a delivery problem, not a parking one. In the 200 mm entrance zone a van corner is 0.46 MPa, factor 3.7. Punching never governs (151 kN at 150 mm against a 10 kN wheel) and subgrade pressure spreads to 49 kPa.

ramp._why: 2.5 m at 1:10. 1.0 m was proposed first and gives 1:4, 14 deg - that is a threshold, not a car ramp. The ramp itself is not what stops you: approach angle is fine at 14 deg for most cars. It is the BREAKOVER at the top. Low saloon 10.2 deg, hatchback 12.5, estate 12.2 - every ordinary car has a breakover under 14, so it drives up and beaches on the crease. At 1:10 the crease is 5.7 deg and everything clears. The extra 1.5 m is 0.67 m3 of concrete, EUR 76.
ramp._isolationJoint: 20 mm compressible joint at the threshold, same as the slab perimeter. The ramp sits at grade and WILL heave in winter; the slab on 150 hardcore inside will not. Cast monolithic and the ramp levers the slab edge every spring.
ramp._transition: Ease the top over 300-500 mm. Even at 5.7 deg a sharp crease is where the surface spalls first - every wheel loads it twice.
ramp._drainage: Fall AWAY at the bottom, or a channel drain. A ramp draining toward the building funnels rain at the one wall with no sill and no piers under it (F8).
ramp._reinforcement: A252 continuous through the ramp. A 2.5 x 3.0 m unreinforced panel sitting on a wedge of fill cracks across the middle.
ramp._fill: 0.94 m3 of wedge fill under it, 250 down to 0 mm, plus 150 hardcore. Compact in 150 mm lifts - it is directly under the thing carrying every wheel that enters.

slab._thicknessDecision: 150 mm CONFIRMED by the owner 2026-08-16. 100 mm was costed at EUR 289 less and would have carried the car perfectly well - driving is an INTERIOR case almost everywhere (0.27 MPa at 100 mm against a 1.73 allowable) and the threshold is covered by the 200 mm entrance zone regardless. What 150 buys is the machine case: a 10 kN foot on a small 100x100 pad near a free edge is 1.97 MPa at 100 mm and OVER, against 0.95 at 150. Plus a thinner slab curls more as it dries, and curled edges are what crack under wheels. Decision closed - thicknessMin 125 is retained only as a record of the calculated floor.
slab._independence: The slab is NOT connected to the pile foundation carrying the frame - confirmed by the owner 2026-08-16. It stops at the wall inner face (y = +-2.85) while the piles sit on the centreline (+-2.925), so there is 75 mm of clear ground plus the 20 mm XPS gap. This is what makes the Westergaard analysis correct rather than optimistic: every figure already treats the perimeter as a free edge carried by the subgrade alone.
slab._pileBackfill: BUILDABILITY: the slab edge runs 75 mm inboard of 24 pile holes, so the slab's worst-loaded zone bears on the ground the piling disturbed. Loose backfill drops the subgrade modulus from about 54 to 20 MN/m3 - edge stress only goes 0.29 -> 0.32 MPa so it does not fail, but the slab deflects more and that is what cracks it over years. Compact the pile-head backfill before the hardcore goes in. Free at the right moment, impossible after.
slab._orderWithRamp: floor 8.61 + ramp 1.12 = 9.73 m3 net, order 10.5 m3 with 7% over.
slab._meshPurpose: The steel is NOT carrying the load checks. Every Westergaard figure in this spec - 0.13 MPa for a car, 0.95 for a machine foot, against 1.73 allowable - was computed on PLAIN concrete. The slab passes with no steel at all.
